newsitem.title: JAPAN: AOL expects return to profitability, end problems.
newsitem.headline: AOL expects return to profitability, end problems.

text.p: Online provider America Online Inc hopes to return to profitability in the second quarter of this year and believes that its highly publicised service problems are behind it, AOL chairman Steve Case said on Monday.
"The general expectation is that we will have a slight loss in the first quarter, and we will generate profit in the April-June quarter," he said.
AOL posted a net loss of $154.8 million in the October-December period of 1996.
Case, in Tokyo to announce the launch of AOL's online service in Japan, also said that he would not comment on market rumours of merger talks with CompuServe Corp, an affiliate of H&R Block Inc.
"We never comment on market rumours," he said.
Industry sources say that AOL, the world's largest online services provider, is involved in talks to buy its beleaguered competitor, possibly in an all-stock transaction.

Despite negative reactions to reports of merger talks, some analysts said a merger could be appealing to AOL because CompuServe has a greater presence internationally, where AOL has been slow to enter.
AOL currently has eight million members worldwide, of which five million are in the United States.
Number two ranked CompuServe has 3.1 million members in the United States and Europe and 2.2 million licenced members in Japan, where it receives royalty payments.
As the first step towards expanding in Asia, AOL announced on Monday that it would launch its online service in Japan on April 15.
AOL will provide the services in Japan through its joint venture with the trading house Mitsui & Co and the business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun Inc.
AOL will charge 980 yen ($7) a month for usage up to three hours and 480 yen ($3) for each additional hour.
Case said that he expects Japan to become the largest market outside of the United States for AOL's online services.
He added he expects similar growth in Japan to what the company has experienced in the United States, where AOL now has five million customers, up from 200,000 five years ago.
Asked about the series of outages that prevented AOL subscribers from accessing their electronic mail, Case said that the system problems were due to the rapid growth in the AOL membership.
He said that the company has been building capacity and hiring more people in the last few months to prevent the problems.
"We believe we've made a lot of progress in dealing with that, and the quality of the service has improved," he said.
The most publicised outage at AOL occurred last August, when the service was down for about 19 hours. AOL said in January it would spend $350 million to upgrade its network.
